motion: It is time for the Arab League to disband

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Tonight's motion is, It is time for the Arab League to disband. Nicholas supports the motion, and Pamela opposes it. Each speaker has thirty seconds to open, followed by two and a half minutes of crossfire. Then each gives a thirty-second closing, with a ten-second cue before each limit. I will enforce those times.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: The Arab League has had decades to turn shared language into dependable action, yet its members still face crises without a united response. A body that cannot coordinate diplomacy, prevent escalation, or deliver meaningful decisions becomes a symbol rather than a solution. Keeping it alive consumes attention that better regional cooperation could use

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Ten seconds please.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Disbanding it would clear space for a smaller, more honest arrangement built around results.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: And let Pamela respond.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: The Arab League is imperfect, but imperfection does not prove that disbanding it is wise. It gives neighboring states a standing forum, preserves communication when relations are tense, and keeps regional concerns visible. Removing that forum would not erase conflict; it would remove one channel for managing it. Reform is difficult, but disappearance is irreversible

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: You have ten seconds.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: A weak institution can be repaired; a vanished institution cannot help anyone. The motion confuses frustration with a sound solution.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: That concludes round one. We're in round two where the debaters are going to be able to talk directly to each other. Two and a half minutes on the clock, starting the moment I stop talking.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: You say the League's forum has value, but a forum that repeatedly produces no common action cannot justify its continued existence. Communication alone is not enough when the structure blocks more effective cooperation.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: No regional institution should ever be abandoned. The League's flaws call for reform, because continuity preserves dialogue that sudden disbanding would destroy.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: You claim continuity preserves dialogue; what concrete function requires this League rather than a redesigned forum with clearer duties and real consequences?

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: This regional institution should be abandoned, but the League should remain. Its problems demand a different structure, not the disappearance of the region's shared table.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: But doesn't your argument for no regional institution should ever be abandoned fight your argument that this regional institution should be abandoned?

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Those statements distinguish a failing structure from the purpose it serves: discard an ineffective institution in principle, while preserving this League's forum through reform. The League can change without vanishing, so I still oppose disbanding it.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: If the League cannot coordinate during a serious regional crisis, disbanding it becomes responsible rather than reckless. That condition is already met whenever members treat its decisions as optional.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: People also argue about its ceremonies and public image, but symbolism is not the central issue. The real question is whether reform can make the forum useful, and that possibility means disbanding it is premature.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Any body that repeatedly fails its essential duty loses its claim to continue, even if some conversations remain useful. A few meetings cannot outweigh a structure that cannot produce collective action.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: If occasional failure makes an institution illegitimate, why should any regional forum survive its first serious crisis, and why not reform the League instead of-

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: I reject that premise: this is not one crisis but a continuing failure. Reform has been the standing excuse, while the League's existence keeps delaying a structure that could actually work.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Imagine rival governments refusing contact after a sudden border clash; the League's permanent channel lets them meet before threats become fighting. That practical contact proves preserving the League can prevent worse harm.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Your example proves only that contact matters, not that this institution must provide it. A hotline, council, or temporary coalition could create contact without preserving a failing shell.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: You dismiss the institution as a shell, but replacing it during a crisis would create dangerous delay and uncertainty. The existing channel is available now, so reform is safer than disbanding it.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Ten seconds left in this round.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: No, keeping an available channel does not prove this League deserves-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: And that's time. And now we move on to round three. And here making his closing statement in support of the motion, Nicholas.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: The strongest point is simple: dialogue is not the same as effective cooperation. Pamela's examples show that contact matters, but they do not show that the Arab League is the right vessel for it. A structure that repeatedly fails to act becomes an obstacle, because it encourages leaders to mistake meetings for progress. Disbanding it would make room for clearer commitments and accountable regional work

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: You've got ten seconds.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: We should preserve the goal of cooperation, not protect an institution merely because it is familiar. The League has had its chance-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Nicholas, that's your time. Thank you. And now, Pamela.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: The League's shortcomings are real, but disbanding it removes a standing channel without guaranteeing anything better. Reform preserves contact, memory, and the possibility of joint action. That is why this institution should change, not disappear.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Thank you both. The debate is closed, with no winner declared.
